title: Katsuta Conquers the Safari: How Kenya's Toughest Rally Finally Gave Up Its Secret
excerpt: Rain, rocks and a dead intercom could not stop Takamoto Katsuta claiming his first World Rally Championship win at Safari Rally Kenya 2026 - and Naivasha has already been confirmed for 2027.
content:
Ninety-four World Rally Championship starts. Plenty of podiums, plenty of speed, and, until March 2026, no victory. Takamoto Katsuta has spent years as the nearly-man of the Toyota Gazoo Racing squad, a driver whose raw pace was never in doubt but whose results rarely matched it. Then came the Safari, the one event on the calendar that punishes impatience more harshly than any other, and the Japanese driver finally delivered.

Katsuta and co-driver Aaron Johnston brought their Toyota GR Yaris Rally1 home 27.4 seconds clear of Hyundai's Adrien Fourmaux after more than three hours and sixteen minutes of competition around Naivasha. Sami Pajari completed the podium in a second Toyota, with Esapekka Lappi fourth for Hyundai. Katsuta became the first Japanese driver to win a round of the World Rally Championship since Kenjiro Shinozuka in 1992 – a gap of more than three decades.

A rally built for survivors

The 2026 Safari, round three of the championship, ran from 12 to 15 March and was shorter and more compact than recent editions. The Kasarani super special was dropped, so for the first time in the modern WRC era the event did not visit Nairobi at all. Instead, everything revolved around the service park at Naivasha: roughly 350 kilometres of competitive driving across 20 special stages, from the volcanic dust of Loldia and Kedong to the open savannah of Soysambu, Elmenteita and Sleeping Warrior, before Sunday's finale through Oserengoni and Hell's Gate.

If the organisers hoped for a tidy, predictable event, the weather had other ideas. Heavy rain arrived for Thursday's opening stage at Camp Moran and turned the Rift Valley soil into a slippery brown paste. Mud packed into radiators – the Hyundais struggled with overheating all weekend – and a stage on Saturday was cancelled as road conditions deteriorated.

Katsuta's nightmare start

Katsuta's rally could easily have ended in the first hour. In the deluge at Camp Moran, his intercom failed, leaving him without Johnston's pace notes for the stage. He lost more than a minute driving essentially blind. On Friday afternoon a double puncture cost him more time, and he went into the overnight halt seventh, almost two minutes off the lead.

Most drivers would have accepted a quiet weekend of damage limitation from there. Instead Katsuta did what the Safari rewards: he drove at a measured pace, kept the car in one piece, and let the rally come to him.

Saturday's carnage

And come to him it did. Saturday on the savannah stages was brutal. The rocky roads around Soysambu, Elmenteita and Sleeping Warrior claimed punctures by the handful – several crews suffered double punctures on the same stage.

  • Elfyn Evans, the championship leader, hit a rock and picked up two punctures; the damage weakened his rear suspension, which failed on the following stage.
  • Thierry Neuville, the reigning world champion, was running second when a run of tyre trouble and mechanical damage ended his day.
  • Sami Pajari had a tyre explode, costing him around five minutes – yet he recovered to win five stages and take third.
  • Sébastien Ogier and Oliver Solberg both stopped on the road section back to service with alternator failures.

By the midday service on Saturday, Katsuta – who had spent Friday fighting his own problems – was leading. He then managed the gap through Sunday's stages to the finish at Hell's Gate, while Solberg salvaged a big haul of Super Sunday and Power Stage points.

The Safari does not reward the fastest driver. It rewards the driver who is still fast when everyone else has stopped.

Fourmaux and Hyundai's consolation

Second place was Hyundai's first podium of the season and a strong drive by Fourmaux and co-driver Alexandre Coria, especially given the cooling problems the i20 N Rally1s endured. Lappi's fourth place was his first points finish at the Safari, a reward for an equally patient approach.

In WRC2, Estonia's Robert Virves won on his first visit to Kenya, beating Gus Greensmith by 30.3 seconds.

How the Kenyans fared

For local fans, the headline was Karan Patel. Co-driven by Tauseef Khan in a Škoda Fabia, the two-time African champion was the top Kenyan, finishing 17th overall and seventh in WRC2, and winning the African Rally Championship category. Aakif Virani, navigated by Zahir Shah, followed him home in 18th. Nikhil Sachania and Deep Patel won the ARC3 class.

Not every Kenyan story was a happy one. Pauline Sheghu and navigator Linet Ayuko, the country's leading women's crew, were forced to retire on Saturday near Eburu after spectators smashed their windscreen and a side window once the rally cars had passed. It was an ugly reminder that the Safari's enormous crowds bring responsibilities as well as atmosphere.

Patel used the Safari as the launchpad for a strong continental season, going on to lead the African Rally Championship standings through the middle of the year.

What it means for Kenyan rallying

The bigger story off the stages was the Safari's place in the world championship. For much of 2026 its future beyond this year was openly in doubt, with the WRC calendar under pressure from new events. That uncertainty has now lifted: the 2027 calendar, expanded to 15 rounds, keeps Safari Rally Kenya as round three, scheduled for 18 to 21 March, again based in Naivasha.

At home, the sport is also getting its house in order. In May 2026 Motorsports Kenya Federation was registered as the national sports organisation for motorsport, following a long governance dispute, and it sanctioned the return of the Kenya National Rally Championship later in the year. For young Kenyan drivers, a stable national series feeding into a secure WRC round is exactly what has been missing.

The Laqim view

Katsuta's win was a perfect Safari story: not the cleanest drive or the fastest, but the most resilient. It is also a reminder of why this event matters. No other round of the championship asks the same questions of a car's suspension, cooling and tyres, or of a crew's patience. The Rift Valley remains the ultimate proving ground – and in March 2027, the world will be back to try again.

title: Importing a Car into Kenya in 2026: The Eight-Year Rule, the Taxes and the Traps
excerpt: From the 2019 registration cut-off to the five taxes that can almost double a car's cost, here is what every Kenyan buyer should understand before a vehicle leaves Japan or the UK.
content:
For most Kenyans, a "new" car is a used import. Japan supplies the overwhelming majority of the vehicles that roll off ships at Mombasa, with the UAE, the UK, Thailand, Singapore and South Africa making up much of the rest. Importing directly can still be the most cost-effective route into a well-specified car – but the rules tightened at the start of 2026, the tax arithmetic is less intuitive than it looks, and mistakes are expensive. Here is how the process works now.

The eight-year rule, rolled forward

Kenya limits used imports to vehicles no older than eight years, enforced through the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) standard KS 1515. In practice, the cut-off is a fixed registration year that moves forward every January. Since 1 January 2026, only vehicles first registered on or after 1 January 2019 are admitted. Cars from 2018 or earlier had to arrive at the port of entry by 31 December 2025; anything later is turned away at the importer's expense.

Two details catch people out:

  • It is first registration that counts, not the year the car was built or the year you bought it. A car manufactured late in 2018 but first registered in 2019 may qualify if the paperwork supports it, so check the export or deregistration certificate carefully.
  • Arrival date matters, not purchase date. If you are buying a car near the oldest permitted year, allow for shipping time. Under the rolling pattern, 2019 vehicles will fall outside the window once the calendar turns to 2027, so anyone eyeing a 2019 car now is cutting it extremely fine.

Kenya drives on the left, and used imports must be right-hand drive. The rules also apply to returning residents and diplomats, though some tax exemptions exist for those groups under conditions set by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA).

Roadworthiness inspection

Every used vehicle must carry a Certificate of Roadworthiness issued before shipment by the KEBS-appointed inspection agency, currently Quality Inspection Services Inc. Japan (QISJ), which operates in the main source markets. The inspection covers age verification, mileage checks, safety items and general condition. A car shipped without the certificate faces delays, re-inspection costs or rejection. Any reputable exporter will arrange this as standard – if one suggests it is optional, walk away.

The five taxes

This is where budgets come undone. KRA does not base duty on what you paid. It works from its own customs value, derived from a Current Retail Selling Price (CRSP) schedule and adjusted for the vehicle's age through a depreciation table. Five charges then apply:

  • Import duty: 35% of the customs value (fully electric cars attract a lower rate).
  • Excise duty: 20% to 35%, charged on the customs value plus import duty. The bands are 20% for engines up to 1,500cc; 25% for petrol and hybrid engines from 1,501cc to 3,000cc and diesels from 1,501cc to 2,500cc; and 35% for petrol engines above 3,000cc and diesels above 2,500cc. Fully electric cars attract a reduced excise rate.
  • VAT: 16%, charged on the customs value plus duty plus excise.
  • Import Declaration Fee (IDF): 3.5% of the customs value.
  • Railway Development Levy (RDL): 2% of the customs value.

Because the taxes stack – excise on top of duty, VAT on top of both – the combined bill commonly lands somewhere between 70% and 100% of the car's customs value. A three-litre petrol SUV pays considerably more, proportionally, than a 1.5-litre hatchback, which is why the 1,500cc and 3,000cc thresholds shape so much of the Kenyan market.

The single most useful number you can get before you buy is KRA's customs value for that exact model, year and engine. Everything else follows from it.

Valuation is still contested

CRSP valuation has been a running dispute. A revised valuation list was suspended by the High Court in 2025, and KRA has said it continues to apply the 2019 CRSP schedule. Even so, importers reported sharp increases in assessed taxes on popular models during 2026. The practical takeaway: get an up-to-date duty estimate from your clearing agent or from KRA for your specific vehicle, rather than relying on a figure from a forum or last year's import.

A note on classics

The Finance Act 2026 introduced a 50% excise rate for antique, vintage and classic vehicles first registered at least 30 years before purchase and valued above KES 10 million. Collectors planning to bring in something special should factor this in.

Beyond tax: the costs people forget

  • Shipping and insurance to Mombasa, usually quoted by the exporter as part of a CIF price.
  • Clearing and forwarding fees, paid to a licensed agent who lodges the entry with customs.
  • Port and container freight station charges, which escalate once the free storage days run out. Delays in paying duty cost money.
  • Registration and number plates through the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA).
  • Transport from Mombasa to Nairobi or upcountry, by road or rail.
  • Immediate servicing: fluids, filters and often tyres, since a car that has sat in a yard and crossed an ocean rarely arrives ready for murram.

Practical advice for buyers

Choose the exporter before you choose the car

Auction-sheet grades and mileage are only as trustworthy as the people reporting them. Use established exporters with a verifiable track record, ask for the original auction sheet and translation, and insist on clear photographs of the underbody.

Think about Kenyan conditions

Japanese-market cars often come on low-profile tyres and soft suspension better suited to smooth expressways than to speed bumps and potholes. Factor in ground clearance, tyre sizes that are readily available locally, and whether parts are stocked by a Kenyan franchise or specialist.

Compare against a locally sold car

Franchise dealers in Kenya sell new and approved used vehicles with warranties and duty already paid. Once all import costs are added, the gap to a dealer car can be narrower than expected – and a local warranty has real value on complex luxury models.

Check before you commit

Import rules, tax rates and valuation schedules in Kenya change, sometimes at short notice and sometimes through court rulings. The figures here reflect publicly reported rates as of November 2026, and further tightening of the age limit has been discussed for future years. Before committing money, confirm the current position directly with KRA (for duty, excise, VAT and valuation) and KEBS (for age limits and inspection requirements), and get a written estimate from a licensed clearing agent.

title: Plugged In: The Honest State of Electric and Hybrid Cars in Kenya
excerpt: With petrol above KSh 226 a litre and a grid powered largely by renewables, the case for going electric in Kenya has never been stronger - but charging, cost and choice still decide who should make the switch.
content:
Kenya has an unusual advantage in the electric car debate. Most of the electricity on its national grid comes from renewable sources – geothermal steam from the Rift Valley above all, with hydro, wind and solar alongside – so an electric car here is cleaner to run than in many of the markets that build them. Add pump prices that have stayed stubbornly high through 2026, and the argument writes itself. Or does it? Here is a clear-eyed look at what is available, what it costs to run, and who should actually make the switch today.

The fuel backdrop

In the pricing cycle from 15 November to 14 December 2026, the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) held Nairobi's maximum pump prices at KSh 226.96 a litre for super petrol and KSh 227.76 for diesel, and that was with the government drawing on the Petroleum Development Levy Fund to cushion an increase. Prices upcountry are higher still. For anyone covering serious mileage, fuel is now one of the largest costs of ownership.

What charging actually costs

Kenya Power offers a dedicated e-mobility tariff for qualifying charging connections. Under the tariff design introduced in 2023, energy is charged at roughly KSh 16 per kWh at peak and around KSh 8 per kWh off-peak – generally overnight on weekdays, with longer windows at weekends. EPRA amended the tariff's consumption threshold in September 2026, replacing a fixed monthly cap with a threshold based on past consumption.

To put that in context, take a mid-sized electric SUV using around 16 to 18 kWh per 100 km. Charged off-peak at about KSh 8 per kWh, 100 km of driving costs in the region of KSh 130 to 150 in energy. A comparable petrol SUV returning 10 litres per 100 km would burn roughly KSh 2,270 of fuel over the same distance at current Nairobi prices. Even at peak rates, or on a standard domestic connection that costs more per unit, the gap is enormous. Public rapid chargers charge commercial rates, so a car that lives on fast charging will cost more to run than one plugged in at home.

The real question is not whether an EV is cheaper per kilometre in Kenya. It is. The question is whether your life fits around where and when you can charge.

The charging map

This is where enthusiasm meets reality. The Electric Mobility Association of Kenya counted around 300 charging points nationally as of mid-2025, concentrated in Nairobi and along major corridors. Kenya Power has been rolling out public stations across several counties, with additions in corridor towns such as Voi and Sabaki on the Mombasa road. Malls, hotels and some fuel stations in Nairobi now host chargers too.

That is progress, but it is not yet a network you can rely on blindly. A Nairobi–Mombasa run is feasible in a long-range EV with planning; a spontaneous trip to Kitale, Lodwar or the Maasai Mara is a different proposition. For most owners, home or workplace charging is the foundation – which rules out many people who live in flats without dedicated parking.

What you can actually buy

New, from franchise dealers

  • BYD arrived in Kenya in 2024 through a CFAO Mobility partnership, launching the Atto 3, Dolphin and Seal. The Atto 3 compact SUV has been advertised at around KSh 8.5 million. The brand has since added the Shark 6 plug-in hybrid pick-up to its line-up.
  • Toyota launched the fully electric bZ4X SUV through CFAO Mobility in 2026, priced at around KSh 10 million, with a claimed range of up to 516 km and an eight-year or 120,000 km battery warranty.

Buying new from a franchise brings warranty cover, trained technicians and a direct line to parts – all particularly valuable with a high-voltage battery.

Used imports

The used market is dominated not by pure EVs but by hybrids. Toyota Aqua, Prius, Corolla and C-HR hybrids, Honda's Vezel and Fit hybrids, and Nissan's Note e-Power are common sights, especially in ride-hailing fleets. Their appeal is simple: they need no charging, return excellent economy in Nairobi's stop-start traffic, and are now a known quantity for local mechanics.

Used imported EVs such as the Nissan Leaf exist, but buyer beware. Battery health matters more than mileage, Kenya's heat is not kind to batteries without active thermal management, and warranty support on a grey import is limited. Insist on a battery state-of-health report before you pay.

Tax and policy

Fully electric cars attract lower import and excise duty rates than petrol and diesel equivalents. In February 2026 the government launched its National Electric Mobility Policy, adding further tax relief on EV components and charging infrastructure. Hybrids, by contrast, are taxed like petrol cars of the same engine size. Policy has been moving in the EV's favour, but Finance Bills are debated every year, so check the current position with KRA before buying.

Who should switch today?

A pure EV makes sense if…

  • You can charge at home or at work, ideally off-peak.
  • Most of your driving is within Nairobi or along well-served corridors.
  • You are buying new with a local warranty, or have a second car for long upcountry trips.

A hybrid makes sense if…

  • You spend hours in city traffic but cannot charge reliably.
  • You regularly drive long distances on roads with no charging.
  • You want lower running costs without changing how you refuel.

Stick with petrol or diesel if…

  • You live or work off-grid, rely on murram and rough tracks, or tow heavily. For deep-rural Kenya, a proven diesel remains the pragmatic tool.

The verdict

Kenya's EV story is moving faster than most people realise, with growing fleets of electric buses, motorbikes and tuk-tuks alongside cars. For private buyers, the economics of electric driving are already compelling; the limiting factor is charging access, not cost per kilometre. If you can plug in at home, an EV is a genuinely sensible choice in 2026. If you cannot, a well-chosen hybrid captures much of the saving with none of the anxiety – and the day when the rest of us can go fully electric is getting closer.

title: The Great Rift Valley Drives: Five Roads Every Kenyan Enthusiast Should Know
excerpt: From the hairpins of the Mai Mahiu escarpment to the flamingo shores of Elementaita, the roads west of Nairobi offer some of the most dramatic driving in Africa - if you time them right.
content:
Leave Nairobi heading west and, within an hour, the ground simply falls away. The Great Rift Valley opens beneath you in a sweep of ochre plains, extinct volcanoes and soda lakes, and the roads that thread through it are some of the most spectacular anywhere. They are also, at times, some of the most demanding. Here is our guide to the best of them, and how to drive them well.

1. The Mai Mahiu escarpment road

The classic. Branching off the Nairobi–Nakuru highway near Limuru, the B3 descends the eastern wall of the Rift towards Mai Mahiu in a sequence of sweeping bends with the valley floor laid out below. Pull in at one of the viewpoints near the top on a clear morning and you can see Mount Longonot's crater and, on a good day, all the way across the valley.

On the way down, look out for the tiny Catholic chapel at the foot of the escarpment. It was completed in late 1942 by Italian prisoners of war, who were also put to work on the road itself, and is now gazetted as a national monument. It is one of the most poignant roadside stops in Kenya.

Driving it well

  • This is a major freight route. Heavily laden lorries crawl up and brake hard on the way down, and impatient overtaking is the real hazard. Be patient, and be visible.
  • Use engine braking on the descent rather than riding the brakes – in an automatic, select a lower gear manually.
  • Morning fog is common at the top of the escarpment, particularly during the rains. Headlights on, speed down.

2. Moi South Lake Road, Naivasha

Once you reach the valley floor and turn towards Naivasha, the Moi South Lake Road loops along the southern shore of Lake Naivasha, past flower farms, acacia woodland and lodges. It is less about speed and more about rhythm: a road to enjoy with the windows down, with giraffe and zebra grazing just beyond the fences of the conservancies.

This is also Safari Rally country. The service park for Kenya's round of the World Rally Championship is based in Naivasha, and the stages at Loldia, Kedong and Oserengoni use the private land around the lake. You will not drive the stages themselves, but you will get a feel for the dust and terrain that the world's best rally drivers face each March.

3. Hell's Gate National Park

Just off the South Lake Road, Hell's Gate is one of the few Kenyan national parks where you can drive, cycle or walk among wildlife. The towering red cliffs, the volcanic plug of Fischer's Tower and the steam rising from the Olkaria geothermal fields make it feel like another planet – it is a landscape that has inspired filmmakers for decades. The park's roads are mostly murram, so it is suited to an SUV or a car with decent ground clearance.

An important note for this season: the Kenya Wildlife Service closed the Hell's Gate gorge in November 2026 because of flash-flood risk during the El Niño rains, which forecasters expect to extend into early 2027. Check the latest status with KWS before you go, and never enter the gorge if rain is falling or forecast on the surrounding hills.

4. Naivasha to Lake Elementaita and Nakuru

Back on the A104 towards Nakuru, the road climbs gently past Gilgil before the shimmering soda flats of Lake Elementaita appear to the left, framed by the profile of the Sleeping Warrior hills. Elementaita, together with Lakes Nakuru and Bogoria, makes up the Kenya Lake System, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its shores are often pink with flamingos.

The surrounding Soysambu Conservancy and the Sleeping Warrior hills will be familiar names to rally fans – they host some of the Safari Rally's most punishing stages. On the public road, the highlight is the view: the stretch between Gilgil and Elementaita offers some of the best panoramas in the Rift.

Continue to Nakuru and you reach Lake Nakuru National Park, renowned for its rhino sanctuary and its birdlife. Allow time, drive slowly on the park roads and remember that animals always have right of way.

5. The long way round: Nakuru to the escarpment and back

For a full-day loop, return to Nairobi on the A104 via Naivasha and climb back up the escarpment to Kijabe and Limuru. The climb out of the valley gives you an entirely different view from the descent, especially in the late afternoon when the sun lights up the western walls. It is a demanding day – around 350 to 400 km depending on detours – so start early.

The Rift Valley rewards the patient driver. The view is always better than the overtake.

Timing your drive

  • Leave Nairobi early. Clearing Westlands and the Waiyaki Way before the morning rush makes an enormous difference. Aim to be on the escarpment by 7am.
  • Avoid Friday evenings and Sunday afternoons on the Nairobi–Naivasha routes, when weekend traffic peaks.
  • Do not plan to drive after dark if you can avoid it. Unlit vehicles, pedestrians, livestock and potholes are far harder to see at night.
  • Watch the season. The long rains (roughly March to May) and the short rains (roughly October to December) can wash out murram roads and bring flash floods. This year's El Niño rains make caution doubly important.

Safety essentials

  • Check tyre pressures and carry a usable full-size spare – sharp volcanic rock is unforgiving.
  • Fill up in Naivasha or Nakuru before heading into parks or conservancies.
  • Respect speed limits and the many speed bumps through towns and trading centres.
  • Carry water, a phone charger and the number of a recovery service you trust.
  • Pay park fees through official KWS channels only.

The Laqim view

You do not need a supercar to enjoy the Rift Valley. You need a well-maintained car, an early start and a willingness to stop when the view demands it. Do that, and these roads will remind you why driving in Kenya can be one of the great pleasures of motoring anywhere.

title: Still the King: Why the Land Cruiser Rules Kenyan Roads - and What Could Dethrone It
excerpt: Range Rover, Lexus LX and Mercedes G-Class all want the Land Cruiser's crown, but on Kenyan murram, the honest comparison comes down to far more than badges and horsepower.
content:
Stand by any major junction in Nairobi for ten minutes and count them. Land Cruisers in every generation – battered 70 Series pick-ups working for county governments and safari outfits, Prados ferrying families to school, and gleaming 300 Series models parked outside the city's best hotels. No other vehicle spans Kenyan society quite like it. The question for anyone spending serious money on a premium 4x4 is whether that reputation is still deserved, or whether the European and Japanese luxury alternatives now offer something better.

Why the Land Cruiser became the default

The Land Cruiser's dominance in Kenya is not about image. It was earned on roads where a breakdown is not an inconvenience but a genuine problem. Three things keep it on top.

  • Durability. Toyota engineers the Land Cruiser for the world's harshest markets – Australia's outback, the Gulf's deserts, Africa's tracks. A body-on-frame chassis, conservative engine tuning and generous cooling margins mean it tolerates abuse that would trouble more delicate machinery.
  • Parts and know-how. Toyota is represented in Kenya by CFAO Mobility, with a dealer network across major towns, and there is hardly a mechanic in the country who has not worked on one. Genuine and quality aftermarket parts are easy to find, even far from Nairobi.
  • Resale value. Land Cruisers hold their value in Kenya like little else, which significantly softens the true cost of ownership.

The current car: Land Cruiser 300

The 300 Series, launched in 2021, moved to the TNGA-F platform and dropped the old V8s for twin-turbo V6 engines. The 3.3-litre diesel develops 227 kW and 700 Nm through a ten-speed automatic, and a 3.5-litre twin-turbo petrol V6 with 305 kW and 650 Nm is offered in some markets. The GR Sport adds the electronically disconnecting stabiliser system (E-KDSS), which lets the anti-roll bars free up off-road for more wheel articulation, plus front, centre and rear locking differentials.

It is more refined than any Land Cruiser before it, and still fundamentally tough. It is not a luxury car in the way a Range Rover is, but the cabin is well built and comfortable for long days on the road.

The rivals

Range Rover (L460)

The Range Rover is the most luxurious vehicle here, and the most comfortable on poor roads. Its air suspension floats over corrugations and potholes with a composure the Toyota cannot match, and the cabin is genuinely special. The 3.0-litre D350 diesel offers 258 kW and 700 Nm; the twin-turbo V8 P530 produces 390 kW and 750 Nm. Jaguar Land Rover is represented locally by Inchcape Kenya.

The trade-off is complexity. Air suspension, sophisticated electronics and expensive parts mean that long-term ownership costs are higher, and the consequences of neglect are more serious. A Range Rover needs a disciplined servicing regime with a specialist who knows the car.

Lexus LX 600

The LX shares its fundamental architecture with the Land Cruiser 300, wrapped in more luxurious trim and with the 3.5-litre twin-turbo V6 petrol engine producing 409 hp (305 kW) and 650 Nm through a ten-speed automatic. In essence, it is a Land Cruiser with a dinner jacket: similar toughness, a quieter and plusher cabin, and the Lexus reputation for build quality.

The catch is that most LX 600s in Kenya arrive as imports, and fuel consumption from the petrol V6 is noticeably higher than the Land Cruiser diesel's. Mechanically, though, much of the support network overlaps with Toyota's.

Mercedes-AMG G 63 and G-Class

The G-Class is the icon, and the facelifted AMG G 63 is absurdly fast for something so upright: a 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 producing 430 kW and 850 Nm, with mild-hybrid assistance. Beneath the AMG theatrics it remains a serious off-roader, with three locking differentials and a 700 mm wading depth. Mercedes-Benz is represented in Kenya by CFAO Mobility.

On a Kenyan road, the G 63 is an occasion rather than a tool. Its fuel consumption is high, its large wheels and low-profile tyres are vulnerable on potholed surfaces, and its purchase price puts it in a different bracket entirely. A non-AMG G-Class is the more rational choice for anyone who actually plans to leave the tarmac.

A Range Rover is the better car to be driven in. A Land Cruiser is the better car to be stranded in – because you are far less likely to be.

The honest comparison for Kenyan conditions

Murram and corrugations

The Range Rover rides best; the Land Cruiser and LX are close behind and less fragile. The G-Class is capable but firm.

Potholes and speed bumps

Sidewall height matters more than anything else. Choose the smallest wheel and tallest tyre offered. Here the Land Cruiser has the edge, as it is commonly specified on more sensible wheel sizes.

Long-distance reliability

The Land Cruiser and LX are the safest bets far from a dealer. The Range Rover and G-Class are dependable when properly maintained, but are less forgiving when things go wrong, and parts may need to be ordered from abroad.

Fuel

The Land Cruiser diesel is the most economical. With pump prices above KSh 220 a litre in Nairobi in late 2026, that is a meaningful saving over thousands of kilometres.

Resale

Nothing beats the Land Cruiser. The LX holds value well; the Range Rover and G-Class depreciate faster, though desirable G 63s can be the exception.

Who should buy what

  • Land Cruiser 300: anyone who regularly drives beyond the tarmac, values peace of mind or plans to keep the car for years.
  • Lexus LX 600: those who want Land Cruiser robustness with more refinement and are happy to pay for petrol.
  • Range Rover: buyers who prioritise comfort and luxury above all, live close to good support and commit to rigorous maintenance.
  • G-Class: buyers who want an icon and have a second vehicle for the hard yards.

The verdict

The rivals beat the Land Cruiser in specific areas – the Range Rover for comfort, the G-Class for presence, the LX for polish. None beats it as a complete package for Kenya. Durability, parts support, economy and resale combine to make it the vehicle every other premium 4x4 here is measured against. Its crown is safe for now.

title: Dust, Murram and Sunshine: The Complete Guide to Looking After a Luxury Car in Kenya
excerpt: Kenyan roads and weather ask more of a fine car than most manufacturers' service schedules assume - here is how to protect the engine, the paintwork and your investment.
content:
A luxury car leaving a factory in Stuttgart, Solihull or Nagoya is engineered for a wide range of conditions. But the service schedule in the handbook is usually written with smooth tarmac, mild temperatures and short distances between dealers in mind. Kenya offers something different: fine volcanic dust, corrugated murram, intense equatorial sunshine, heavy seasonal rain and some of the most unforgiving speed bumps anywhere. None of this needs to frighten you. It simply means looking after a car here with a little more thought.

Understand "severe service"

Almost every manufacturer publishes two maintenance schedules: a normal one and a "severe" or "harsh conditions" one. Dusty roads, frequent short trips, extended idling in traffic and high ambient temperatures all appear on the severe list – which describes a typical week of Nairobi driving followed by a weekend upcountry. If your car spends real time in these conditions, follow the severe schedule, even if your dealer's service reminder suggests otherwise. It usually means shorter intervals for engine oil, air filters and some fluids.

Dust: the silent enemy

Kenyan dust is extraordinarily fine, particularly the pale volcanic soils of the Rift Valley. It finds its way everywhere.

  • Engine air filter. Inspect it at every service, and more often after murram trips. A clogged filter starves the engine, while a damaged one lets abrasive dust in, which is far worse.
  • Cabin air filter. Replace it more often than the schedule suggests. A blocked cabin filter strains the air-conditioning blower and fills the car with dust and odours.
  • Brakes. Dust accelerates wear on pads and discs and can cause squealing. Have the brakes cleaned and inspected regularly.
  • Seals and joints. Driveshaft boots, suspension bushes and wheel bearings all suffer. Ask your technician to inspect them during each service.

Murram, potholes and speed bumps

Rough roads place heavy loads on suspension, steering and tyres. Simple habits make a big difference:

  • Slow right down for speed bumps, and cross them at a slight angle in low cars to avoid scraping the front splitter or exhaust.
  • Use raised ride heights where fitted. Air suspension on a Range Rover, Mercedes or Porsche is designed for exactly this; use the higher settings on rough roads and lower them again on the highway.
  • Have alignment checked after any heavy pothole strike, and as routine every few months. Misalignment destroys expensive tyres quickly.
  • Listen for new knocks from the suspension. Early attention to a worn bush or link is far cheaper than chasing the damage it causes later.

Tyres: your most important upgrade

Many luxury cars arrive in Kenya – especially as Japanese or UK imports – on large wheels with low-profile tyres. They look superb and ride poorly on broken roads, and their sidewalls offer little protection against sharp potholes.

  • Where the manufacturer approves it, consider a smaller wheel with a taller tyre. It improves ride, reduces the risk of rim damage and often makes tyres cheaper.
  • Check pressures weekly, cold, using the figure on the door pillar. Underinflated tyres are more vulnerable to pothole damage and overheating.
  • Watch for ageing as well as wear. Strong sunshine accelerates rubber degradation, so inspect sidewalls for cracking and pay attention to the manufacture date on the tyre.
  • Carry a usable spare. A tyre repair kit is no help with a sidewall split on a remote road.

Fuel quality

Buy fuel from busy, reputable stations, where stock turns over quickly and the risk of contamination is lower. If your car's handbook calls for higher-octane petrol, use the premium grade where available. Modern direct-injection engines and diesels with particulate filters are sensitive to fuel quality; if you notice rough running, hesitation or warning lights after filling up, have it checked promptly rather than driving on.

Diesel owners should be aware that cars which only ever do short city trips may struggle to complete particulate filter regeneration. A regular longer run at steady highway speeds helps keep the system healthy.

Heat and sunshine

  • Cooling system. Coolant should be renewed to schedule using the correct specification. Check levels regularly and look for leaks.
  • Battery. Heat shortens battery life. Have it tested before long trips, especially if the car is two or three years old.
  • Interior. Ultraviolet light fades and cracks leather and dashboards. Use a windscreen sunshade, park in the shade whenever possible, and condition leather regularly.
  • Air-conditioning. Have it serviced periodically so it keeps working efficiently through hot months and traffic jams.

Protecting the paintwork

Paint has to endure intense sunshine, stone chips from murram, bird droppings, tree sap and sometimes enthusiastic but rough hand-washing.

  • Paint protection film on the bonnet, front bumper and mirrors is the most effective defence against stone chips.
  • Ceramic coatings add UV resistance and make the car easier to clean.
  • Wash correctly. Rinse off dust before touching the paint, use clean microfibre mitts and avoid dry-wiping dusty panels, which creates swirl marks.
  • Remove bird droppings and sap quickly. In hot sunshine they can etch clear lacquer within days.

Servicing: where and how often

For cars under warranty, use the franchise dealer to protect your cover. Outside warranty, a reputable independent specialist who knows your brand can be excellent value – ask about the diagnostic equipment they use, whether they fit genuine or OEM-quality parts, and whether they keep detailed records. A full, documented service history adds significantly to resale value in Kenya.

The cheapest maintenance is the service you do on time. The most expensive is the one you postponed.

The Laqim checklist

  • Follow the severe-service schedule if you drive in dust, traffic or heat.
  • Inspect air filters often; replace the cabin filter generously.
  • Check tyre pressures weekly and alignment after any heavy impact.
  • Choose sensible wheel and tyre sizes for Kenyan roads.
  • Fuel at reputable, busy stations, using the grade your handbook specifies.
  • Protect the paint with film, coatings and careful washing.
  • Keep every receipt and stamp: a documented history pays for itself.

Treat a fine car with that kind of care and it will repay you with years of the refinement and performance you bought it for – whatever the road throws at it.

title: From a Shed in Nakuru to the Safari: Inside Laqim Racing and Laqim Rally
excerpt: Two free browser games bring Kenyan roads, Kenyan stories and genuine rally spirit to any screen - no download, no console, just a link and a lot of dust.
content:
Most racing games are set somewhere else. You lap the Nordschleife, slide through Monte Carlo or blast along Californian highways – magnificent places, but not ours. Laqim Racing and Laqim Rally were built to change that. They are free, they run in your web browser, and every corner of them is drawn from Kenya: the escarpment, the coast, the Rift Valley, the city at night and the spirit of the Safari Rally.

Both games are available now at laqimautoworld.com/play/. There is nothing to install and nothing to pay. Here is what is waiting for you.

Laqim Racing: six Kenyan-inspired tracks in 3D

Laqim Racing is the circuit and road racer of the pair – quick to pick up, satisfying to master and built around six tracks that each capture a different side of the country.

Laqim Circuit

The home track. A purpose-built circuit of fast sweepers, heavy braking zones and a tight final complex, it is the place to learn each car's limits and set the lap times your friends will chase.

Rift Valley Trail

Red earth, acacia country, two mud bogs and a river crossing. This is the dirt track, and it rewards SUVs and lifted builds; a low sports car will spend half the lap fighting for grip.

Nairobi Night Run

A tight street circuit under the lights, lined with concrete walls and no run-off. Boda bodas and matatus run along the service road beside it, and one touch of the wall ends a fast lap.

Diani Coast Road

Palms, the Indian Ocean, dhows and kitesurfers offshore, and sea-breeze sand blowing across two apexes. Diani rewards rhythm, and punishes anyone who brakes on the sand.

Hell's Gate Gorge

Red murram between volcanic cliffs, with zebra and giraffe on the gorge floor and geothermal vents blowing steam straight across the road. Drive into the steam and you lose sight of the road for a moment.

Thika Superhighway

The newest track: 4.2 km of closed-off expressway with two flat-out straights over a kilometre long and two heavy-braking hairpins. Bring the fastest car you have.

Laqim Rally: a career with a story

If Laqim Racing is about lap times, Laqim Rally is about a journey. Its story career starts in the humblest possible place – a shed in Nakuru, a tired car and a dream – and builds towards the biggest event in African motorsport: the Safari Rally.

Guiding you is Mzee Joseph Kamau, the seasoned mentor who takes a raw young driver under his wing. His guidance is the heart of the story. Standing in your way is Jabari Kitur, the gifted rival whose speed forces you to raise your game at every turn. Their rivalry gives the career a purpose beyond chasing times: every stage moves the story on.

Start with nothing in Nakuru. Finish on the Safari. Everything in between is up to you.

Game modes that only Kenya could inspire

Alongside the career, Laqim Rally offers a set of modes that turn familiar Kenyan experiences into driving challenges.

  • Game Drive – no stopwatch, just a camera. Find zebra, giraffe, wildebeest and elephants on the Maasai Mara, approach slowly and stop for the photo. Charge in and the herd scatters.
  • Balloon Chase – dawn over the Mara. Stay close to a drifting hot-air balloon as the chase crew and be at the basket when it lands.
  • Rhino Charge – inspired by the real charity event: six guard posts out in the bush, reached in any order. The shortest distance wins.
  • Kasarani Super Special – one night run on a stadium stage in Nairobi, in front of a full crowd, against your rival’s time.
  • Clinic Run – carry vaccines across the north to a clinic by Lake Turkana, fast but gently, before the ice packs melt.

Laqim Racing has its own set of modes too, including Safari Endurance: six laps with tyres that wear out and one compulsory pit stop.

Open-world Nakuru

Between events, Laqim Rally lets you loose in an open-world Nakuru: the town and its market, the A104 highway with its long straights, the Industrial Area and the shore of Lake Nakuru with its flamingos. Matatus and boda bodas share the road. Drive to a marker and the story comes to you: parts runs for Mzee, highway duels with your rival Jabari Kitur, promotional runs for sponsors, a tow job, a hospital dash for Mama Wairimu’s daughter. Every job pays, and every chapter moves the career forward.

Why we built them

Laqim Autoworld exists to celebrate the cars and driving culture of Kenya. The games are an extension of that: a way for anyone – whether they own a dream car, are saving for one or simply love motorsport – to experience the thrill of Kenyan roads. They are also a way to share the Safari story with a new generation of fans who may never have stood at the side of a stage in Naivasha.

Tips for new players

  • Start on Laqim Circuit to learn braking points and car behaviour before tackling Hell's Gate Gorge.
  • In the career, follow the story. Mzee Kamau's guidance and Jabari's challenges are there to push you towards the Safari.
  • Smooth is fast. Over-driving on loose surfaces costs more time than it gains, exactly as it does in the real Safari.
  • Explore Nakuru. Story missions in the open world add depth to the career and reward curiosity.
  • Save Safari Endurance for later. In Laqim Racing it tests everything you have learned.

And there is more

Racing and rally are not the only games in the garage. Laqim Football brings the same quick, free, browser-based approach to the beautiful game – ideal for a break between stages.

Ready to play?

All the Laqim games are free to play at laqimautoworld.com/play/ in any modern web browser. Pick your track, pick your car – or step into the shed in Nakuru and begin the long road to the Safari. Mzee Kamau is waiting, and Jabari will not wait for anyone.

title: Beyond the Safari: A Fan's and Competitor's Guide to Kenyan Motorsport
excerpt: The national rally championship is back, autocross is thriving and the Rhino Charge just raised a record sum - here is how Kenya's motorsport scene works and how to become part of it.
content:
The World Rally Championship's annual visit to Naivasha grabs the headlines, and rightly so. But Kenyan motorsport is far more than one weekend in March. Behind the Safari sits a network of clubs, national championships, grassroots events and one of the most extraordinary charity competitions in the world. After a turbulent period off the stages, 2026 has been a year of rebuilding. Here is how the scene fits together – and how to get involved.

A new governing body

For several years, Kenyan motorsport was hampered by a governance dispute. In 2025 the Sports Disputes Tribunal ruled that the Kenya Motor Sports Federation had lost its recognition because it had not converted from a company structure into a national sports organisation as the Sports Act 2013 requires. In May 2026, after a High Court appeal was dismissed, Motorsports Kenya Federation was registered as the national sports organisation for motorsport, with former Safari Rally winner Carl "Flash" Tundo as interim chair.

The new body's stated priorities include holding elections, aligning with the FIA (motorsport's world governing body) and reviving the national rally championship. Motorcycle sport is governed separately by the Motorcycle Sports Federation of Kenya.

The Kenya National Rally Championship

The KNRC is the backbone of the domestic scene – the series where Kenya's leading drivers cut their teeth and where young talent is spotted. Uncertainty around the championship's administration led several top Kenyan crews, including Karan Patel, to focus on the FIA African Rally Championship in 2026.

The KNRC returned with a season opener at Stoni Athi, south-east of Nairobi, on 31 July and 1 August 2026, organised by the 254 Motorsports Club. Motorsports Kenya Federation waived entry fees for that first round to encourage a strong field. Rounds are hosted by affiliated clubs across the country, and the calendar can shift, so follow the federation and the clubs for confirmed dates.

The African stage

Kenyans have been prominent in the African Rally Championship. Patel, a two-time African champion, led the 2026 standings after winning Rwanda's Mountain Gorilla Rally in July, with fellow Kenyan Aakif Virani second at that point. The Safari itself counts towards the ARC, which is why Kenyan crews run in a dedicated category alongside the WRC field.

Autocross: where most careers start

If rallying is the dream, autocross is the doorway. Events take place on short, purpose-made dirt courses, with cars running against the clock in heats. Costs are a fraction of rallying, the action is compact and spectator-friendly, and classes cater for everything from everyday saloons to purpose-built buggies. Stoni Athi has become a regular venue; it hosted the first autocross under the new federation in May 2026.

Autocross is also where many of Kenya's rally drivers began – learning car control on loose surfaces long before they tackled a forest stage.

Hill climbs and sprints

Hill climbs and time trials appear periodically on club calendars, with drivers tackling a closed uphill course one at a time against the clock. Naivasha's Malewa Bay and the Aberdare foothills have both hosted events in the past. They are relaxed, family-friendly days out and an excellent way to see a wide variety of machinery up close.

The Rhino Charge

There is nothing else quite like it. Founded in 1989 and organised by the conservation trust Rhino Ark, the Rhino Charge is an off-road competition with a single purpose: raising money to protect Kenya's mountain forests and water towers, including the Aberdares, Mount Kenya and Mau Eburu.

How it works

  • Teams must visit 13 guard posts scattered across around 100 square kilometres of brutal terrain within 10 hours.
  • The winner is the team that completes the course over the shortest distance, measured by GPS – not the fastest. Choosing to winch straight up a gorge rather than drive around it is part of the strategy.
  • The venue changes every year and is kept secret until the event, so no one can scout it in advance.
  • Entries are capped at 65 vehicles to limit environmental impact, and each team must meet a minimum fundraising pledge.

The 2026 edition, the 37th, raised a record KSh 365 million for conservation. The event is usually held around late May or early June.

Only in Kenya would the winning car be the one that drove the least distance.

How to get involved as a fan

  • Go to the Safari. Spectator areas at stages such as Hell's Gate and the savannah stages around Naivasha offer an unforgettable view. The 2027 event is scheduled for 18 to 21 March. Use official spectator points, follow marshals' instructions and never stand on the outside of a bend.
  • Watch a national round. KNRC events and autocross meetings are far less crowded and give you a close-up view of the cars and crews.
  • Join a club. Club membership gives you access to events and the paddock community. Many clubs need volunteers, and that is the best way in.
  • Become a marshal. Every event depends on trained volunteers to keep it safe. Marshalling puts you closer to the action than any spectator and gives you a deep understanding of the sport.
  • Respect the cars and crews. At the 2026 Safari, a Kenyan crew was forced to retire after spectators damaged their car. Fans make the event; they also have a duty to protect it.

How to get involved as a competitor

  • Start with autocross. It is the most affordable way to learn car control and race craft.
  • Get licensed. Competition licences are issued through the national federation; you will need to meet safety equipment and medical requirements.
  • Invest in safety first. An approved helmet, a FIA-homologated seat and harness, and a properly certified roll cage come before performance upgrades.
  • Find a co-driver and a crew. Rallying is a team sport. Experienced navigators and mechanics are as important as the driver.
  • Budget realistically. Tyres, fuel, entry fees, spares and travel add up quickly. Sponsorship from local businesses is common and worth pursuing.

The road ahead

Kenyan motorsport is entering a promising phase. The Safari has a confirmed place on the 2027 World Rally Championship calendar, the national championship has restarted under new governance, and grassroots events are attracting fresh talent. Whether you want to watch from a hillside in Naivasha, volunteer with a stopwatch at a guard post or strap into a car yourself, there has rarely been a better moment to get involved.

title: Toyota Land Cruiser 300 Review: The Benchmark Kenyan 4x4, Judged on Kenyan Roads
excerpt: Twin-turbo V6 power, a stronger chassis and decades of hard-won reputation make the Land Cruiser 300 the yardstick for every premium off-roader in Kenya.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Toyota Land Cruiser 300 (GR Sport / ZX)

Laqim score: 9/10

For

  • Proven toughness on murram and corrugations
  • Strong, frugal 3.3 V6 diesel
  • Unrivalled parts support and resale value in Kenya

Against

  • Not as plush as a Range Rover on broken tarmac
  • Bulky in Nairobi traffic and parking
  • Strong demand keeps prices high

The Land Cruiser 300 is not the most luxurious 4x4 you can buy in Kenya, but it is the one most likely to do everything you ask of it for the longest time.

Introduction

Some cars are reviewed. The Land Cruiser is measured. Across Kenya, from ministry convoys to Maasai Mara lodges and Nairobi's most exclusive driveways, it has become the default answer to the question "What do you need?" The 300 Series is the latest chapter, launched in 2021, and it carries a heavy burden of expectation. We have looked at the two versions Kenyan buyers ask about most: the off-road-focused GR Sport and the luxury-oriented ZX.

Design and interior

The 300 is square-shouldered and imposing, with a tall bonnet and upright glasshouse that give excellent visibility – a genuine safety asset on Kenyan roads. The GR Sport wears a blacked-out grille with bold TOYOTA lettering and a more muscular look; the ZX is chromier and more formal.

Inside, the cabin is a major step forward over the 200 Series. A large central touchscreen, physical controls for the climate and four-wheel-drive systems, and well-bolstered seats make it a comfortable place for long days. Quality is robust rather than lavish: the plastics are hard-wearing, the switchgear feels built to last, and nothing rattles on corrugated roads. Seven-seat versions are common, though the third row is best kept for shorter journeys.

Performance and how it drives

The 300 Series replaced the old V8s with twin-turbocharged V6 engines. The 3.3-litre diesel produces 227 kW and 700 Nm, the latter from just 1,600 rpm, and drives through a ten-speed automatic. Australian-market figures quote 0–100 km/h in 7.9 seconds for the GR Sport diesel and combined fuel consumption of around 8.9 L/100 km. A 3.5-litre twin-turbo petrol V6, with 305 kW and 650 Nm, is offered in some markets and appears on some ZX imports.

On the road the diesel is the pick. It pulls effortlessly from low revs, overtakes with authority on the Nairobi–Nakuru highway and settles into a relaxed cruise. The ten-speed gearbox is smooth, if occasionally busy on hills. Steering is light and slow by car standards, but precise enough for a vehicle of this size, and body control is much better than older Land Cruisers.

Off-road, the 300 is outstanding. Low-range gearing, multi-terrain modes, crawl control and locking differentials – front, centre and rear on the GR Sport – give it formidable ability. The GR Sport's E-KDSS system electronically disconnects the anti-roll bars for extra wheel articulation on rough ground, then reconnects them for stability on the highway.

GR Sport or ZX?

The choice comes down to how you use the car. The GR Sport is the one for owners who genuinely venture off the tarmac: E-KDSS and the full set of locking differentials make a measurable difference on rough, rutted tracks. The ZX majors on comfort and equipment and suits buyers whose driving is mostly city and highway, with the occasional gravel road. Both share the same fundamental toughness, so neither is a wrong answer.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

This is home ground. The 300 absorbs corrugated murram at sensible speeds with a calm, controlled ride, and the body-on-frame construction shrugs off the punishment that wears out monocoque SUVs. It is the car you would choose for a long run to Samburu or the Mara.

Potholes and speed bumps

The tall tyres on standard wheels make it very forgiving. Larger optional wheels look good but reduce that margin; we would stick to the smaller sizes.

Nairobi traffic

Its size is the weakness. Squeezing through tight mall car parks and Westlands side streets takes care, although cameras and parking sensors help. In stop-start traffic the diesel is smooth and refined.

Highway cruising

Quiet, stable and relaxed. Wind noise is well suppressed and the long gearing helps economy. It is a superb long-distance machine.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

Toyota is represented in Kenya by CFAO Mobility, with a dealer network across the country. That matters: genuine parts, trained technicians and diagnostic equipment are within reach in most major towns, and independent Toyota specialists are everywhere.

  • Fuel: the diesel is the economical choice. With diesel at KSh 227.76 a litre in Nairobi in the November–December 2026 pricing cycle, the difference over the petrol V6 adds up quickly.
  • Servicing: follow Toyota's severe-conditions schedule if you use the car on dusty roads – most Kenyan owners will.
  • Tax: both engines sit in the top excise band for imports (diesel above 2,500cc; petrol above 3,000cc).
  • Resale: exceptionally strong. Few vehicles in Kenya lose value more slowly.

Rivals

  • Lexus LX 600: shares the platform with more luxury and a thirstier petrol engine.
  • Range Rover: far more comfortable and luxurious, but more complex and costly to maintain.
  • Mercedes-Benz G-Class: more iconic and more expensive, firmer-riding and thirstier in AMG form.
  • Toyota Land Cruiser 250 (Prado): the smaller, cheaper sibling, and for many families the more sensible buy.

Verdict

The Land Cruiser 300 is not perfect. A Range Rover rides better, an LX feels more special, and a G-Class turns more heads. But on Kenyan roads none of them combines toughness, ability, economy, parts support and resale as completely. Choose the diesel, resist the biggest wheels, and you have the most rounded premium 4x4 in the country.

Specifications vary by market and model year, so check the exact figures for any car you are considering, especially imports.

title: Range Rover (L460) Review: The Finest Luxury SUV on Kenyan Roads - With Conditions
excerpt: Air suspension that floats over potholes and a cabin that rivals a limousine make the fifth-generation Range Rover a sublime place to cover Kenyan kilometres, provided you commit to its upkeep.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Range Rover (L460)

Laqim score: 8.5/10

For

  • Best ride quality of any SUV on broken Kenyan tarmac
  • Beautiful, serene and spacious cabin
  • Genuinely capable off-road on air suspension

Against

  • Complex systems demand disciplined maintenance
  • Higher running and repair costs than Japanese rivals
  • Depreciates faster than a Land Cruiser

The L460 Range Rover is the most comfortable and luxurious way to travel on Kenyan roads, but it rewards owners who maintain it meticulously and live near good support.

Introduction

Since 1970 the Range Rover has occupied a unique position: a car equally at home outside a Karen garden party and on a muddy farm track in the highlands. The fifth generation, codenamed L460, arrived in 2022 and is the most refined and technologically advanced yet. In Kenya, where the roads can switch from smooth dual carriageway to broken tarmac within a kilometre, its talents are particularly relevant – and so are its demands.

Design and interior

The L460 is a masterclass in reduction. Flush door handles, a clean, unbroken waistline and slim lights give it a sculpted, almost monolithic look that ages well. It is available in standard and long-wheelbase forms, the latter offering seven seats or a lavish four-seat layout.

Inside, it is the most luxurious cabin in its class. Materials are rich, the seats are superb over long distances and the driving position commands the road. A large curved touchscreen runs the infotainment, while climate controls remain easy to use. Refinement is exceptional: at highway speeds wind and road noise are so well suppressed that conversation never needs to rise above a murmur.

Performance and how it drives

Engine choice varies by market, but the core line-up includes:

  • D350: 3.0-litre six-cylinder mild-hybrid diesel, 258 kW and 700 Nm.
  • P460e: plug-in hybrid combining a petrol six with an electric motor, 339 kW and 550 Nm combined; 0–100 km/h in 5.7 seconds.
  • P530: 4.4-litre twin-turbo V8, 390 kW and 750 Nm; 0–100 km/h in about 4.6 seconds and a top speed of about 250 km/h.
  • SV P615: the flagship V8, 452 kW and 750 Nm.

For Kenyan buyers, the D350 is the sweet spot: abundant torque for effortless overtakes, strong range and lower fuel costs than the V8. The V8 is magnificent – smooth, muscular and quick for something of this size – but its thirst is significant at current pump prices.

On the road, the Range Rover is about serenity. Air springs front and rear and adaptive dampers give a ride that floats over imperfections, while all-wheel steering makes it more manoeuvrable in town and more stable at speed than its size suggests. It is not a sports car, and does not pretend to be, but it is composed, precise and deeply relaxing to drive.

Off-road, the Terrain Response system and adjustable ride height make it more capable than most owners will ever need. Raise the suspension, select the right mode and it climbs, wades and crawls with ease.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

Few vehicles ride corrugations as well. The air suspension isolates the cabin superbly, and at sensible speeds the Range Rover feels unflustered on long murram runs. The concern is longer-term: dust and repeated impacts place stress on air-suspension components, which need inspection and, eventually, replacement.

Potholes and speed bumps

The suspension copes beautifully, but the large wheels – often 22 or 23 inches – are vulnerable. Choose the smallest wheel and tallest tyre available. Raising the ride height for rough sections helps protect the underbody.

Nairobi traffic

Elevated, quiet and calm, it is an excellent place to sit in a jam. Rear-wheel steering helps in car parks, though its width still demands care on narrow roads.

Highway cruising

Outstanding. Long trips to Mombasa or Kisumu pass with remarkable ease, and the D350's range means fewer fuel stops.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

Jaguar Land Rover is represented in Kenya by Inchcape Kenya, giving owners access to franchise servicing, genuine parts and factory diagnostics. For a car this complex, that matters enormously.

  • Servicing: follow the manufacturer's schedule strictly, and use the severe-conditions intervals if you drive on dusty roads. Air filters and suspension components deserve particular attention.
  • Parts: some items may need to be ordered from abroad, so budget for waiting times as well as costs.
  • Fuel: the diesel is the most economical choice; the V8 is costly at current prices.
  • Warranty: buying new or approved used through the franchise is strongly advisable. An extended warranty is worth considering.
  • Resale: values fall faster than those of the Land Cruiser or Lexus LX.
A Range Rover is a magnificent car to own. It is a less magnificent car to neglect.

Rivals

  • Toyota Land Cruiser 300: tougher, cheaper to run and with stronger resale, but noticeably less refined.
  • Lexus LX 600: Land Cruiser underpinnings with luxury and Lexus reliability; less comfortable on broken roads.
  • Mercedes-Benz G-Class: more iconic and rugged in feel, firmer-riding and less spacious.
  • Mercedes-Benz GLS and BMW X7: similar luxury, less off-road ability.

Verdict

On sheer quality of experience, the L460 Range Rover is the best luxury SUV you can drive on Kenyan roads. It rides with uncanny calm, its cabin is a genuine sanctuary and it is far more capable off-road than its elegance suggests. The cost of that sophistication is complexity, and complexity demands care. Buy it from the franchise, choose the diesel, keep to the schedule, and it is a superb companion. Treat it like a Land Cruiser, and you will regret it.

Specifications vary by market and model year; confirm the exact powertrain and equipment of any car you are considering.

title: Lexus LX 600 Review: A Land Cruiser in a Dinner Jacket
excerpt: The LX 600 pairs Land Cruiser 300 toughness with Lexus luxury and a twin-turbo V6 - a compelling package for Kenya, with one or two caveats about fuel and support.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Lexus LX 600

Laqim score: 8.5/10

For

  • Land Cruiser-grade durability beneath the luxury
  • Quiet, beautifully finished cabin
  • Strong 409 hp twin-turbo V6

Against

  • Thirsty petrol engine at Kenyan pump prices
  • Most cars arrive as imports rather than through a local franchise
  • Infotainment and ergonomics trail European rivals

The LX 600 is the most robust luxury SUV you can buy for Kenya, offering Land Cruiser peace of mind with a markedly more special cabin - if you can live with its fuel bills.

Introduction

Walk around the forecourts of Kenya's premium used-car dealers and you will see a lot of LX 600s. It is not hard to see why. The fourth-generation LX, launched in 2021, is built on the same TNGA-F body-on-frame platform as the Toyota Land Cruiser 300, and shares much of its mechanical DNA. For buyers who want luxury without abandoning the Land Cruiser's reputation for indestructibility, it is an obvious candidate. The question is whether it is more than a Land Cruiser with a fancier badge.

Design and interior

The LX's spindle grille dominates the face, and the styling is more ornate than the Land Cruiser's square-jawed look. It is undeniably imposing, and in F Sport form it gains a sportier edge. Body panels are unique to the Lexus, so it does not read as a rebadged Toyota.

The cabin is where the LX justifies itself. Leather quality, stitching, wood and metal finishes are a clear step up from the Land Cruiser, and the dual-screen layout – an upper screen for navigation and media and a lower one for climate and off-road information – works well in practice. Refinement is excellent, with impressive isolation from wind and road noise. Some markets offer an "Ultra Luxury" four-seat version with reclining rear seats, a genuine rival to chauffeur-driven saloons.

The weak points are relatively minor: the infotainment software is less intuitive than the best European systems, and some switchgear is shared with cheaper Toyotas.

Performance and how it drives

The LX 600 uses a 3.5-litre twin-turbo V6 petrol engine producing 409 hp (305 kW) and 650 Nm from 2,000 rpm, driving all four wheels through a ten-speed automatic. Lexus quotes a top speed of 210 km/h in Middle Eastern specification. A hybrid LX 700h has more recently joined the range in some markets.

On the road, the V6 is smooth and strong, pulling the LX's considerable mass with ease. Overtaking on the Mombasa road is effortless, and the gearbox shifts smoothly. Adaptive variable suspension gives a comfortable, controlled ride, and the LX feels more cushioned than the Land Cruiser, though it never quite matches a Range Rover's air-sprung float.

Off-road, the LX inherits the Land Cruiser's essential capability: low-range gearing, multi-terrain management and serious traction systems. Ground clearance is generous, and the body-on-frame construction tolerates punishment. Most owners will never explore its limits, but it is reassuring to know they are there.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

Like the Land Cruiser, the LX handles corrugated murram calmly and is built to keep doing so for years. It is an excellent choice for owners with upcountry homes or regular trips to conservancies.

Potholes and speed bumps

The ride is forgiving, but be wary of large-wheeled versions. Smaller wheels with taller tyres are the better option for Kenyan conditions.

Nairobi traffic

It is a large car, so tight parking and narrow side streets require patience. In traffic it is quiet and comfortable, but the petrol V6 burns fuel quickly in stop-start conditions.

Highway cruising

Superb. Quiet, stable and fast, with a 110-litre fuel tank that helps compensate for its thirst on long trips.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

We could not confirm a current authorised Lexus franchise in Kenya; most LX 600s on Kenyan roads arrive as imports from Japan, the UAE or elsewhere. In practice, the mechanical overlap with the Land Cruiser 300 helps considerably – many components and much of the technical know-how are shared with Toyota, and experienced Toyota and Lexus specialists are found across Nairobi. Before buying, check how any warranty would be honoured locally.

  • Fuel: the petrol V6 is the LX's biggest running cost. With super petrol at KSh 226.96 a litre in Nairobi in late 2026, high-mileage owners should budget carefully.
  • Tax: the 3.5-litre petrol engine falls in the top excise band for imports (above 3,000cc).
  • Servicing: follow Lexus's severe-conditions schedule if you drive on dusty roads.
  • Resale: strong, helped by its Land Cruiser connection, though not quite at Land Cruiser levels.
The LX's greatest luxury is not the leather. It is the confidence that it will get you home.

Rivals

  • Toyota Land Cruiser 300: nearly as capable, more economical with the diesel, far easier to buy through a Kenyan franchise and cheaper.
  • Range Rover (L460): more luxurious and comfortable, but more complex and costly to maintain.
  • Mercedes-Benz GLS and G-Class: strong brand appeal and official Kenyan representation; the GLS is less rugged, the G-Class firmer-riding.
  • BMW X7: more dynamic on tarmac, much less suited to rough roads.

Verdict

The LX 600 is a genuinely compelling choice for Kenya. It delivers real luxury and refinement without sacrificing the robustness that makes the Land Cruiser so trusted. It is thirsty, and buying through official channels is less straightforward than for a Toyota, but for buyers who want a luxury SUV that will tolerate years of Kenyan roads, it has few equals. If you do not need the extra polish, the Land Cruiser 300 diesel remains the wiser buy; if you do, the LX is the one to have.

Specifications and equipment vary by market and model year, so check the details of any imported car carefully.

title: Mercedes-AMG G 63 Review: The Icon, Turned Up to Eleven
excerpt: A hand-assembled twin-turbo V8, three locking differentials and a silhouette unchanged in spirit since 1979 - the G 63 is gloriously absurd, and more capable in Kenya than its image suggests.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Mercedes-AMG G 63

Laqim score: 8/10

For

  • Unmistakable presence and character
  • Ferocious V8 performance with mild-hybrid help
  • Genuine off-road hardware beneath the glamour

Against

  • Very high fuel consumption
  • Large wheels and low-profile tyres are vulnerable on potholes
  • Firm ride and modest space for its size

The G 63 is an extraordinary indulgence that is genuinely capable off-road, but on Kenyan roads it is best enjoyed as an occasion rather than relied on as a daily tool.

Introduction

The Mercedes-Benz G-Class began life in 1979 as a military and utility vehicle. More than four decades later, its AMG G 63 incarnation is one of the most desirable status symbols in the world, and Nairobi is no exception. The latest facelift, introduced for the 2025 model year, brought mild-hybrid technology, a revised interior and an optional active suspension system. It is easy to be cynical about a car like this. It is also very hard not to grin when you drive it.

Design and interior

The shape is the point. Flat panels, upright glass, exposed door hinges, round headlights and the spare wheel on the tailgate – it looks like nothing else on the road. AMG adds a vertical-slat grille, side-exit exhausts and large wheels. Doors still close with a distinctive, solid clack.

Inside, the dashboard is dominated by wide digital displays for instruments and infotainment, with high-quality leather, metal and carbon trim. The upright driving position and narrow cabin give a commanding but slightly old-fashioned feel. Rear-seat space and boot volume are adequate rather than generous for a car of its footprint – a GLS or Range Rover is far roomier.

Performance and how it drives

The G 63's 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 produces 430 kW and 850 Nm, and a 48-volt mild-hybrid system can add up to 15 kW and 200 Nm on demand. Mercedes' published figures, as reported, put 0–100 km/h at around 4.1 seconds with the optional AMG Performance Package, and a claimed top speed of 240 km/h. The mild-hybrid model weighs around 2,640 kg.

Those numbers barely capture the experience. The V8 is thunderous, pulling with relentless force and accompanied by a soundtrack that turns heads across a car park. The nine-speed automatic shifts quickly, and on a clear stretch of highway the G 63 gathers speed with a violence that seems to defy physics.

The optional AMG Active Ride Control replaces conventional anti-roll bars with hydraulically interconnected dampers, reducing body roll dramatically on tarmac and loosening off for articulation off-road. Even so, the G 63 is a tall, heavy vehicle with a high centre of gravity, and it rewards smooth, measured inputs rather than hard cornering.

Off-road, the hardware is genuine: three locking differentials, a low-range transfer case, a 700 mm wading depth and the ability to climb 45-degree slopes. Few owners will test it, but a G 63 with suitable tyres is a formidable off-roader.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

The chassis is tough enough, but the ride is firm and the large wheels transmit more of the surface into the cabin than a Land Cruiser or Range Rover. Slow down and it copes; push on and it becomes uncomfortable.

Potholes and speed bumps

This is the G 63's weak spot. Low-profile tyres on the larger optional wheels, up to 22 inches in many markets, leave little protection against sharp pothole edges. If you plan to use the car outside Nairobi's best roads, choose the smallest wheel available, or consider a non-AMG G-Class on more sensible tyres.

Nairobi traffic

Its upright shape and good visibility make it easier to place than its bulk suggests. But the V8 is thirsty in stop-start driving, and its firm ride is noticeable over Nairobi's rumble strips.

Highway cruising

Fast and stable, though wind noise from the upright body is greater than in more aerodynamic rivals. Long journeys are comfortable enough, if not serene.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

Mercedes-Benz is represented in Kenya by CFAO Mobility, so official servicing, genuine parts and factory diagnostics are available – an important advantage for a car with this much technology.

  • Fuel: expect heavy consumption, especially in town. At Nairobi's late-2026 pump prices of more than KSh 226 a litre for petrol, this is a significant running cost.
  • Tyres and wheels: large performance tyres are expensive and pothole damage is a real risk.
  • Servicing: follow the schedule strictly, and pay close attention to air filters and brakes in dusty conditions.
  • Tax: the 4.0-litre petrol engine falls into the top excise band for imports.
  • Resale: desirable G 63s hold their value better than most high-performance SUVs, though specification and condition matter enormously.
No one buys a G 63 because they need one. They buy it because nothing else makes them feel quite the same.

Rivals

  • Lamborghini Urus SE: faster and sharper on tarmac, far less capable off it.
  • Range Rover (L460): more comfortable and spacious, with a more refined character.
  • Lexus LX 600: less exciting, far more economical to run and more forgiving on rough roads.
  • Mercedes-Benz G 500 / G 450 d: the same icon with more rational running costs.

Verdict

The G 63 is not a rational purchase, and it does not need to be. It is an icon with real substance: a genuine off-roader with a monstrous V8 and an aura no rival can match. On Kenyan roads, though, its firm ride, thirst and vulnerable tyres make it a car best enjoyed alongside a more practical daily vehicle. If you want a G-Class for real-world use here, the non-AMG versions make more sense. If you want the ultimate expression of the legend, nothing else will do.

Specifications vary by market and model year; check the details of any car you are considering.

title: Porsche 911 Turbo S (992) Review: The Everyday Supercar Meets Kenyan Reality
excerpt: Now hybrid-assisted and more potent than ever, the 911 Turbo S is the most usable supercar money can buy - but Kenyan speed bumps and support networks demand careful thought.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Porsche 911 Turbo S

Laqim score: 8.5/10

For

  • Staggering, all-weather performance
  • Remarkably usable and comfortable for a supercar
  • Superb build quality and engineering

Against

  • Low nose and wide tyres versus Kenyan speed bumps and potholes
  • Official support network in Kenya needs checking
  • Very expensive tyres, brakes and servicing

The 911 Turbo S is the most complete everyday supercar in the world, but in Kenya it suits owners with good roads, a front-axle lift and a trusted specialist.

Introduction

For five decades, the 911 Turbo has been Porsche's answer to a deceptively simple question: how fast can a car be while remaining comfortable, reliable and usable every day? The 992-generation Turbo S answers it more convincingly than ever. The original 992 Turbo S arrived in 2020; the updated version, revealed at the IAA Mobility show in Munich in September 2025, adds a T-Hybrid powertrain and even more performance. Both are extraordinary machines. The question for a Kenyan buyer is how much of that brilliance survives local roads.

Design and interior

The 911's silhouette remains instantly recognisable, but the Turbo S is wider, with large intakes ahead of the rear wheels, active aerodynamics and a broad rear wing. It looks muscular rather than flamboyant – a car that conveys its performance quietly.

The cabin is classic modern Porsche: a low, perfect driving position, a curved digital instrument display, high-quality leather and metal, and excellent ergonomics. Physical switches for key functions remain, which is a blessing. The rear seats are for children or bags, but the front luggage compartment and rear seat space make it more practical than most supercars.

Performance and how it drives

The latest T-Hybrid

The updated Turbo S uses a 3.6-litre flat-six combined with Porsche's T-Hybrid system: two electric exhaust turbochargers, a 1.9 kWh high-voltage battery and an electric motor integrated into the eight-speed PDK gearbox. Porsche quotes 523 kW (711 PS) and 800 Nm, 0–100 km/h in 2.5 seconds for the coupé and a top speed of 322 km/h. It weighs around 85 kg more than its predecessor, yet lapped the Nürburgring Nordschleife about 14 seconds faster.

The earlier 992 Turbo S

The first 992 Turbo S, from 2020, uses a 3.7-litre twin-turbo flat-six producing 478 kW (650 PS) and 800 Nm, with 0–100 km/h in 2.7 seconds and a 330 km/h top speed. In Kenya, where many 911s arrive as imports, this is the version buyers are most likely to encounter.

On the road, both are astonishing. Acceleration is brutal and immediate, all-wheel drive delivers traction in any weather, and the PDK gearbox shifts almost instantly. Yet the Turbo S remains calm and docile at low speeds, with a ride that is firm but well damped and a cabin quiet enough for long journeys. It is a car that can cross a continent in comfort and then dominate a circuit.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

This is not a murram car. It can cope with short, well-graded gravel at low speeds, but dust, stones and corrugations will chip the paint, stress the suspension and invade the cabin. Paint protection film on the nose is essential.

Potholes and speed bumps

The biggest challenge. The low nose and splitter are vulnerable to Kenya's steep speed bumps, and the large wheels and low-profile tyres offer limited protection against sharp potholes.
