Porsche's optional front-axle lift, available on many 911s, raises the nose at the touch of a button and is close to mandatory here. Cross bumps slowly and at an angle.

Nairobi traffic

Surprisingly easy. The 911 is compact by supercar standards, the visibility is good and the PDK is smooth in crawling traffic. The challenge is the unexpected pothole or unmarked bump, not the congestion itself.

Highway cruising

A delight on good tarmac. Stable, quiet and effortless, though open stretches should always be driven within the law and with an eye on livestock, pedestrians and slower vehicles.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

The previous operator of Porsche Centre Nairobi lost the franchise in 2021. Before buying, confirm the current authorised Porsche service partner in Kenya through Porsche's official dealer locator. For a car with hybrid systems, complex electronics and very specific maintenance requirements, access to factory diagnostics and trained technicians is critical.

  • Tyres and brakes: high-performance tyres and large brakes are expensive to replace. Ceramic brakes in particular are costly if damaged.
  • Fuel: the Turbo S requires premium petrol; use reputable stations.
  • Servicing: follow Porsche's schedule strictly and use a specialist with the correct diagnostic equipment.
  • Tax: at 3.6 and 3.7 litres, the engine falls into the top 35% excise band for imported petrol cars above 3,000cc.
  • Insurance: premiums for cars of this value and performance are significant; secure parking helps.
The Turbo S does not ask you to compromise your daily life for performance. Kenyan roads, however, may ask you to compromise a little.

Rivals

  • Nissan GT-R Nismo: similar all-weather, all-wheel-drive approach with more raw character and less refinement.
  • Mercedes-AMG GT: more grand-touring in feel, also widely available as an import.
  • McLaren Artura and Ferrari 296 GTB: more exotic and dramatic, less usable every day.
  • Lamborghini Urus SE: an SUV alternative with similar pace and far better ground clearance.

Verdict

The 911 Turbo S is one of the great all-round performance cars, and the T-Hybrid version raises the bar further. In Kenya it works brilliantly for owners who drive mostly on good tarmac, specify the front-axle lift, protect the paint and have access to a trusted Porsche specialist. For anyone who regularly faces murram or rough roads, a Cayenne or Urus makes more sense. But if you want supercar performance you can genuinely use every day, there is nothing better.

Specifications differ between model years and markets; confirm the exact details of any car you are considering.

title: Lamborghini Urus SE Review: The Super-SUV Goes Electric-Assisted
excerpt: With 588 kW from a twin-turbo V8 and an electric motor, the plug-in hybrid Urus SE is the fastest way to arrive anywhere in Kenya that has a decent road to it.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Lamborghini Urus SE

Laqim score: 8/10

For

  • Supercar acceleration with SUV ground clearance
  • Plug-in hybrid allows quiet electric running in town
  • Outrageous design and presence

Against

  • No confirmed official Lamborghini dealer in Kenya
  • Large wheels and performance tyres suffer on rough roads
  • Running costs on a supercar scale

The Urus SE is the most usable Lamborghini ever built and a genuine super-SUV, but in Kenya it is a car for good roads and owners prepared to manage support themselves.

Introduction

When Lamborghini launched the Urus in 2018, purists were horrified. A Lamborghini SUV? Then it became the most successful model in the company's history. The Urus SE, revealed in 2024, is the brand's first plug-in hybrid super-SUV and replaced the original petrol-only models. It combines a reworked twin-turbo V8 with an electric motor to deliver more power, more torque and the ability to glide silently through town. In Kenya, where Lamborghinis are rare sights, it is the model most likely to make sense for real-world use. But does it?

Design and interior

The Urus SE sharpens the original's angular design with a new bonnet, redesigned headlights with Lamborghini's Y-shaped signature and a revised rear. It remains unmistakable: low, wide and aggressive for an SUV, with a stance that suggests a supercar on stilts.

Inside, the cabin is dramatic and driver-focused, with a fighter-jet-style starter switch under a red flip cover, a large central touchscreen and high-quality leather and Alcantara. The seats are supportive and comfortable, and the rear has genuine space for adults. The boot is practical, although the hybrid battery takes some space compared with the earlier petrol model.

Performance and how it drives

The Urus SE uses a 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 producing 456 kW and 800 Nm, paired with an electric motor of 141 kW and 483 Nm integrated into the eight-speed automatic gearbox. Combined output is 588 kW (800 CV) and 950 Nm. Lamborghini quotes 0–100 km/h in 3.4 seconds, 0–200 km/h in 11.2 seconds and a top speed of 312 km/h. A 25.9 kWh battery gives up to around 60 km of electric-only driving. A sharper Urus SE Performante has since joined the range.

The performance is ferocious. The V8 and electric motor deliver an almost seamless surge from any speed, accompanied by a thunderous soundtrack in Sport and Corsa modes. Yet in electric mode the Urus SE becomes almost serene, gliding through city traffic in silence – a remarkable contrast.

Air suspension, active anti-roll and rear-wheel steering give it astonishing agility for a car of its size and weight. It corners flatly, steers precisely and grips tenaciously. Off-road modes allow it to tackle gravel and mild tracks, and the air suspension can raise the body for clearance, but it is designed primarily for tarmac.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

It will manage well-graded murram at moderate speeds, especially with the suspension raised. But the performance tyres and large wheels are not designed for repeated punishment, and dust and stones will challenge the paintwork. Paint protection film is essential.

Potholes and speed bumps

The adjustable ride height is a big advantage over low supercars. Speed bumps pose few problems in the higher setting. Potholes are the bigger concern: low-profile tyres on 21- to 23-inch wheels leave little margin.

Nairobi traffic

Electric mode is a genuine asset. Crawling through Westlands or Upper Hill silently, with no fuel burned, is a unique Urus SE party trick. The car's width and attention-grabbing design make parking more of a concern than the traffic itself.

Highway cruising

Fast, stable and surprisingly comfortable in Strada mode, though road noise from the wide tyres can be noticeable on coarse surfaces.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

We could not confirm a current authorised Lamborghini dealer in Kenya, so most cars arrive as private imports. That has important consequences for warranty, diagnostics and parts. Owners should establish a relationship with a qualified specialist, consider an official Lamborghini service centre in the wider region for major work, and confirm how warranty claims will be handled before buying.

  • Charging: charging at home, ideally off-peak, makes the most of the electric range. Kenya Power's e-mobility tariff offers reduced overnight rates for qualifying connections.
  • Fuel: the V8 is thirsty when used hard; electric running in town reduces consumption significantly.
  • Tyres and brakes: large performance tyres and carbon-ceramic brakes are expensive to replace.
  • Tax: as a hybrid with a 4.0-litre petrol engine, it is taxed in the top excise band for imports.
  • Insurance and security: significant premiums and secure parking are part of ownership.
The Urus SE is two cars in one: a silent city cruiser and a 312 km/h missile. Kenya's roads decide which one you use more often.

Rivals

  • Mercedes-AMG G 63: more iconic and far more capable off-road, slower and cruder on tarmac.
  • Porsche Cayenne Turbo E-Hybrid: similar technology, more understated and more broadly supported.
  • Range Rover (L460) P530 or SV: more luxurious and comfortable, much less sporting.
  • Aston Martin DBX707 and Ferrari Purosangue: equally exotic, equally rare on Kenyan roads.

Verdict

The Urus SE is a technical tour de force: supercar performance, genuine everyday usability and the ability to run silently on electricity in town. In Kenya, its adjustable ride height makes it far more practical than a low-slung supercar, but its performance tyres, large wheels and lack of confirmed local franchise support mean it suits owners with good roads and a dependable specialist. For those buyers, it is a thrilling, uniquely theatrical way to travel.

Specifications vary by market and model year; confirm the details of any car you are considering.

title: Rolls-Royce Ghost Series II Review: Silence, Effortlessness and a Very Long Bonnet
excerpt: The Ghost is Rolls-Royce's most driver-focused saloon, with a 6.75-litre V12 and a ride tuned to erase imperfections - an exquisite machine that asks Kenyan roads to be on their best behaviour.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Rolls-Royce Ghost Series II

Laqim score: 8/10

For

  • Unmatched refinement and ride comfort
  • Effortless V12 performance
  • Exquisite craftsmanship and personalisation

Against

  • Low-profile tyres and long overhangs versus potholes and speed bumps
  • No confirmed authorised Rolls-Royce dealer in Kenya
  • Ownership costs on a different scale

The Ghost Series II is perhaps the most serene car in the world, and on Kenya's better roads it is sublime, but owners must plan carefully for support and protect it from the worst surfaces.

Introduction

The Ghost is the most understated saloon in the Rolls-Royce range – less ostentatious than the Phantom, more personal than the Cullinan, and designed for owners who enjoy driving themselves as much as being driven. The second-generation Ghost arrived in 2020, and the Series II update in 2024 refreshed its design and technology. Kenya has long had a small but devoted Rolls-Royce community, so the question is less whether it is a magnificent car – it is – and more how well it suits life here.

Design and interior

The Ghost Series II features slimmer, more angular headlights, a revised illuminated Pantheon grille and a cleaner rear. The proportions are classic Rolls-Royce: long bonnet, long wheelbase and a sense of quiet, unhurried power. At more than 5.5 metres long in standard form, it is a substantial presence on any street. An Extended version adds rear legroom for those who prefer to be driven.

Inside, craftsmanship is extraordinary. Leather is soft and flawless, wood veneers are book-matched and the "Starlight" headliner can recreate a night sky above the occupants. Series II introduced the latest digital interface and connectivity, with the optional illuminated fascia adding a glowing design across the dashboard. Personalisation is almost limitless: owners can specify colours, materials and details unique to their car.

Performance and how it drives

The Ghost uses a 6.75-litre twin-turbo V12 producing 571 hp (420 kW) and 850 Nm from just 1,600 rpm, driving all four wheels through an eight-speed automatic. Published figures give 0–100 km/h in 4.8 seconds and an electronically limited top speed of 250 km/h, impressive for a car weighing around 2,490 kg.

Yet speed is not the point. The V12 delivers effortless, near-silent progress, with the gearbox using satellite-navigation data to select the right gear for the road ahead. All-wheel steering makes this large car more manoeuvrable than expected, while the "Planar" suspension system, with an upper wishbone damper and a forward-looking camera that reads the road surface, aims to deliver the celebrated "magic carpet ride". Refinement is extraordinary, with remarkable isolation from wind, road and engine noise.

Driven briskly, it is composed and secure, if never sporting. The Black Badge version adds more power and a sharper character for those who want a darker, more dynamic Ghost.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

This is not what the Ghost was designed for. Short sections of well-graded gravel at walking pace are fine, but corrugations and dust are the enemies of a car whose entire purpose is serenity – and stones will damage paintwork that may represent a substantial part of its value.

Potholes and speed bumps

The suspension absorbs ordinary imperfections superbly, but sharp potholes remain a threat to large wheels and low-profile tyres, and the long overhangs require care over steep speed bumps. Experienced chauffeurs approach them slowly and at an angle.

Nairobi traffic

A wonderfully calm place to sit, with the cabin sealing occupants away from the noise outside. Its length makes tight parking, narrow streets and some hotel driveways challenging.

Highway cruising

On a smooth highway the Ghost is sublime, covering long distances with almost no sense of effort. Rough or broken stretches reduce the experience considerably.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

We could not confirm a current authorised Rolls-Royce dealer in Kenya, so most cars arrive as private imports. Owners need a clear plan for maintenance: a qualified specialist locally, and access to an authorised Rolls-Royce service centre in the wider region for warranty work and major servicing. Confirm how warranty and parts supply will be handled before you buy.

  • Fuel: the V12 is thirsty, particularly in town; budget accordingly at current pump prices.
  • Tyres and suspension: premium tyres are expensive, and suspension components are complex.
  • Tax: the 6.75-litre engine falls into the top excise band for imports.
  • Insurance and security: premiums are high and secure parking is essential.
  • Chauffeur training: if the car will be driven for you, ensure the driver understands its size, weight and the care needed over speed bumps.
A Rolls-Royce is not measured in kilometres per hour. It is measured in decibels – and the Ghost has very few of them.

Rivals

  • Bentley Flying Spur: more sporting and dynamic, with a similarly lavish cabin.
  • Mercedes-Maybach S-Class: superb comfort and technology, with official Mercedes-Benz representation in Kenya.
  • Rolls-Royce Cullinan: the same luxury with far better ground clearance – arguably the more sensible Rolls-Royce for Kenya.
  • Range Rover SV: high luxury with genuine rough-road ability.

Verdict

The Ghost Series II is one of the most refined cars on earth, combining effortless V12 performance with craftsmanship few manufacturers can match. On Kenya's best roads it is a profound pleasure, whether you drive or are driven. But its low-profile tyres, long overhangs and lack of confirmed local franchise support mean ownership demands planning. For many Kenyan buyers, the Cullinan's higher ride height will make more practical sense. For those who want the purest expression of Rolls-Royce luxury, the Ghost remains in a class of its own.

Specifications and options vary by market; confirm the details of any car you are considering.

title: Nissan GT-R Nismo Review: Farewell to Godzilla, the Japanese Legend Kenyans Still Crave
excerpt: R35 production ended in 2025 after 18 years, making the 600 hp GT-R Nismo an instant collector's car - and one of the most intense driving machines you can bring to Kenya.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Nissan GT-R Nismo

Laqim score: 7.5/10

For

  • Ferocious all-wheel-drive performance
  • Hand-built VR38 twin-turbo V6 and huge character
  • Rising collector status now production has ended

Against

  • Very firm ride on Kenyan roads
  • Low nose and stiff suspension versus potholes and speed bumps
  • Specialist parts and expertise needed

The GT-R Nismo is a brutally fast, deeply characterful collector's car, but in Kenya it is a weekend and track-day machine rather than an everyday companion.

Introduction

When the R35 Nissan GT-R launched in 2007, it rewrote the supercar rulebook: a four-seat Japanese coupé that could match or beat cars costing far more, in any weather. Its nickname, Godzilla, carried over from earlier Skyline GT-Rs and stuck. In August 2025, after 18 years and roughly 48,000 cars, the final R35 rolled off the line in Tochigi, Japan. The Nismo, tuned by Nissan's motorsport division, is the ultimate version – and now, with production over, an instant collector's item. Kenyan enthusiasts have always loved the GT-R. Here is how it fares on Kenyan roads.

Design and interior

The GT-R's design has always been functional rather than beautiful, and the Nismo takes that further. Carbon-fibre bumpers, side skirts and a large rear wing – revised for the final models with a larger surface area on swan-neck mounts – give it purposeful, aggressive aerodynamics. Lightweight RAYS wheels and red accents complete the look.

The interior shows its age. Recaro bucket seats are superb, holding you firmly in place, and the Alcantara-trimmed steering wheel is excellent. But the infotainment and much of the switchgear are clearly from an older generation, and the rear seats are suitable only for small children or bags. It is a driver's car, not a luxury car.

Performance and how it drives

At the heart of the Nismo is the 3.8-litre twin-turbo VR38DETT V6, hand-assembled by a small team of specialist technicians. In Nismo form it produces 600 hp (about 441 kW) at 6,800 rpm and 652 Nm between 3,600 and 5,600 rpm, using turbochargers derived from Nissan's GT3 racing programme. Drive goes through a six-speed dual-clutch transmission to all four wheels; kerb weight is around 1,754 kg. For the 2024 model year, the Nismo gained a front limited-slip differential for the first time.

On the road it is ferocious. The V6 builds boost with a mechanical, industrial snarl before the GT-R launches forward with violent, relentless acceleration, and the all-wheel-drive system finds traction on almost any surface. Steering is heavy and precise, body control is iron-fisted and the brakes are immense. It is a car that rewards commitment and punishes carelessness.

That intensity has a price. The ride is very firm, the gearbox can be clunky at low speeds, and road noise is considerable. This is a car that never lets you forget its purpose.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

Avoid them. The stiff suspension and low ride height make murram deeply uncomfortable, and stones will damage the bodywork and carbon components.

Potholes and speed bumps

This is the GT-R's greatest challenge in Kenya. The front splitter sits low, the suspension is unforgiving and the 20-inch wheels, with tyres of 255/40 at the front and 285/35 at the rear, offer little protection against sharp pothole edges. Cross speed bumps slowly and at an angle, and plan routes carefully.

Nairobi traffic

Possible, but not enjoyable. The firm ride, low-speed gearbox behaviour and heat build-up in traffic make the Nismo a poor choice for daily commuting.

Highway cruising

Stable and fast on smooth tarmac, though noisy and firm over long distances. The 74-litre fuel tank helps, but this is no grand tourer.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

The GT-R Nismo arrives in Kenya as a private import, typically from Japan, the UAE or the UK. Owners should establish a relationship with a specialist who has experience of the VR38 engine and the GT-R's transmission, and should budget for parts to be sourced from abroad.

  • Fuel: the GT-R requires high-octane premium petrol; use reputable stations.
  • Servicing: the transmission and engine require specialist care, and fluid changes are critical. Follow the manufacturer's schedule strictly.
  • Tyres and brakes: performance tyres wear quickly and are expensive; the brakes are large and costly to replace.
  • Tax: the 3.8-litre petrol engine falls in the top excise band for imports, and the eight-year rule means only cars first registered from 2019 onwards can be imported in 2026.
  • Value: with production ended, well-maintained, low-mileage Nismos are likely to be sought after by collectors. A full service history is essential.
The GT-R was never about luxury. It was about how much speed engineering could squeeze from every kilogram – and the Nismo squeezed hardest of all.

Rivals

  • Porsche 911 Turbo S: faster, more refined and more usable every day, but far less raw.
  • BMW M3 Competition xDrive: more practical and comfortable, with official BMW support in Kenya.
  • Mercedes-AMG GT: more grand-touring in character, with a V8 soundtrack.
  • Toyota GR Yaris: far slower but cheaper, more usable and arguably as entertaining on a twisty road.

Verdict

The GT-R Nismo is the final, most extreme form of a modern legend. It is brutally fast, deeply engaging and, now that production has ended, increasingly collectable. But it is also firm, noisy and ill-suited to the realities of everyday Kenyan driving. As a weekend car for good roads and track days, it is thrilling. As a daily companion, look elsewhere.

title: BMW M3 (G80) Review: The Super-Saloon That Does Everything
excerpt: With up to 530 hp, all-wheel drive and four proper doors, the updated M3 Competition M xDrive is a supercar-baiting saloon you can use every day in Nairobi - and it has official backing in Kenya.
content:
Verdict at a glance

BMW M3 Competition M xDrive (G80)

Laqim score: 8.5/10

For

  • Blistering performance with everyday practicality
  • Superb chassis and all-wheel-drive traction
  • Official BMW franchise support in Kenya

Against

  • Firm ride on broken roads, even in Comfort
  • Low-profile tyres vulnerable to potholes
  • Divisive grille design

The G80 M3 is the most complete performance car for Kenyan buyers who want speed and practicality in one package, provided they respect its low-profile tyres.

Introduction

For almost four decades, the BMW M3 has defined the performance saloon. The G80 generation, launched in 2020 and updated in 2024, is the most powerful and technologically advanced M3 yet, and the first offered with all-wheel drive. In Kenya, where many enthusiasts need one car that can do the school run, the office commute and a weekend blast to Naivasha, it makes an unusually strong case.

Design and interior

The G80's large vertical kidney grille divided opinion at launch, and still does. Beyond it, the M3 is muscular and purposeful: flared arches, deep air intakes, a carbon roof on many versions and quad exhausts. The 2024 update brought revised lights and detail changes. In darker colours and with the right wheels it looks menacing; in brighter shades the grille dominates.

The interior is excellent. The curved display combining the digital instruments and central touchscreen is clear and quick, though more functions now sit in menus than before. M Sport seats – or the optional carbon bucket seats – hold you tightly, and the M steering wheel, with red M1 and M2 shortcut buttons for favourite settings, is a highlight. Crucially, there are four doors, five seats and a usable boot.

Performance and how it drives

The M3 uses a 3.0-litre twin-turbo straight-six. In the updated M3 Competition M xDrive, it produces 530 hp (390 kW) at 6,250 rpm and 650 Nm between 2,750 and 5,730 rpm, driving through an eight-speed M Steptronic automatic. BMW quotes 0–100 km/h in 3.5 seconds and a top speed of 250 km/h, rising to 290 km/h with the M Driver's Package. Rear-wheel-drive versions, including a six-speed manual in some markets, remain available, and an M3 Touring estate exists too.

On the road it is spectacular. The straight-six is responsive and loves to rev, the gearbox is quick and smooth, and the M xDrive system gives astonishing traction while still allowing the car to feel rear-biased and playful. A 2WD mode disconnects the front axle entirely for experienced drivers on track. Steering is precise, body control is excellent and the brakes are powerful and consistent.

In everyday driving, Comfort mode softens the adaptive dampers enough for city use, the gearbox shifts smoothly and the exhaust settles down. It is a remarkably civilised car when you want it to be.

Which M3 for Kenya?

For most Kenyan buyers, the Competition M xDrive is the one to have. All-wheel drive makes its performance accessible on wet tarmac during the rains, and the automatic suits Nairobi traffic. The rear-drive manual is the purist's choice and a joy on a dry mountain road, but it demands more skill and offers less margin when conditions turn slippery.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

Short stretches at slow speed are manageable, but the M3's low ride height and firm suspension make longer murram drives uncomfortable, and stones will chip the paint. Paint protection film on the nose is a wise investment.

Potholes and speed bumps

The low front splitter and staggered wheels – 19-inch at the front and 20-inch at the rear on many cars – are vulnerable. Speed bumps need slow, careful approaches, and sharp potholes can damage rims and tyres. Keep pressures correct and plan routes where possible.

Nairobi traffic

Easy and comfortable in Comfort mode, with good visibility and a smooth automatic. It is much less demanding in traffic than a supercar.

Highway cruising

Fast, stable and relaxed on good tarmac. Road noise from the wide tyres is noticeable on coarse surfaces, but long trips are comfortable.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

BMW is represented in Kenya by Inchcape Kenya, which provides franchise servicing, genuine parts and factory diagnostics – a clear advantage over the many performance cars that arrive as private imports.

  • Fuel: the M3 requires premium petrol and is thirsty when driven hard, but reasonably efficient when cruising.
  • Tax: the 3.0-litre engine sits just inside the 25% excise band for imported petrol cars up to 3,000cc, rather than the top 35% band – a notable advantage over larger-engined rivals.
  • Servicing: follow BMW's schedule, and pay attention to air filters and brakes on dusty roads.
  • Tyres and brakes: performance tyres and the optional carbon-ceramic brakes are expensive to replace.
  • Warranty: buying through the franchise is strongly advisable for a car this complex.
The M3 asks you to make almost no compromises – except at the speed bump.

Rivals

  • Mercedes-AMG C 63 S E Performance: plug-in hybrid with huge power, but heavier and more complex.
  • Audi RS models: strong all-weather pace and understated style.
  • Nissan GT-R Nismo: faster, rawer and far less practical.
  • BMW M5: larger, more powerful and more luxurious, at a much higher price.

Verdict

The G80 M3 is one of the most complete performance cars on sale. It is extraordinarily fast, engaging and practical, and in Kenya it benefits from official BMW franchise support. Its firm ride and low-profile tyres demand respect on rough roads, but for buyers who want a car that can be both a family saloon and a weapon on the weekend, few can match it.

title: Toyota GR Yaris Review: A Rally Car for the Road, Built for Roads Like Ours
excerpt: Developed with lessons from the World Rally Championship and now with 280 hp and an optional eight-speed automatic, the GR Yaris may be the most fun you can have on a Kenyan road.
content:
Verdict at a glance

Toyota GR Yaris

Laqim score: 9/10

For

  • Rally-bred all-wheel drive that thrives on loose surfaces
  • Compact, agile and endlessly entertaining
  • Toyota's mechanical reputation and support network

Against

  • Firm ride and road noise on long trips
  • Cramped rear seats and small boot
  • Limited availability; often an import

The GR Yaris is a genuine homologation-inspired rally car for the road, perfectly suited to Kenya's mix of tarmac and gravel, and the most engaging car here per shilling.

Introduction

In March 2026, Takamoto Katsuta won Safari Rally Kenya in a Toyota GR Yaris Rally1. The road car that shares its name is not the same machine, of course, but it was born from the same ambition. Toyota developed the GR Yaris as a road-going car shaped by its World Rally Championship programme, with a bespoke three-door body, a carbon-composite roof and a sophisticated all-wheel-drive system. The car was updated in 2024 with more power, a stiffer body and a new automatic option. For Kenyan enthusiasts, few cars feel more relevant.

Design and interior

The GR Yaris looks nothing like an ordinary Yaris. Its roof is lower, its arches are wider, and the three-door body is unique to this model. The 2024 update added a new lower grille, repositioned rear lights and a revised front bumper designed for better cooling. It looks compact, muscular and purposeful – a car that wears its rally intentions openly.

The updated cabin is a major improvement. A new 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster, a dashboard angled towards the driver and a driving position lowered by 25 mm give it a far more focused feel. Sports seats are supportive, and the controls feel solid. The rear seats are cramped, and the boot is small, but this is a car bought for driving rather than carrying.

Performance and how it drives

The GR Yaris uses a 1.6-litre turbocharged three-cylinder engine. In its updated form it produces 280 hp (206 kW) at 6,500 rpm and 390 Nm between 3,250 and 4,600 rpm. Buyers can choose a six-speed manual or the new eight-speed GR automatic, developed with input from professional drivers. Toyota quotes weights of around 1,280 kg for the manual and 1,300 kg for the automatic.

The GR-FOUR all-wheel-drive system is the star. It offers three modes – Normal, Sport and Track – which vary the front-to-rear torque split. On tarmac it feels agile and adjustable; on gravel it comes alive, finding traction where most cars would slide and allowing the driver to steer the car on the throttle in a way that feels genuinely rally-inspired.

The engine is punchy and rev-happy, with a gruff three-cylinder character. Steering is sharp and communicative, the chassis is beautifully balanced and the 2024 body reinforcements – including more spot welds and structural adhesive – give it greater precision. It is fast, but above all it is fun at speeds that are realistic and responsible on public roads.

Kenyan roads

Murram and corrugations

Here the GR Yaris shines. Its all-wheel drive and compact size make it confident and enjoyable on well-graded gravel. Ground clearance is still limited compared with an SUV, so take care on deeply rutted or rocky tracks, and protect the paint with film if you plan to explore regularly.

Potholes and speed bumps

The firm suspension and low-profile tyres require attention. The GR Yaris clears most speed bumps more easily than a supercar, but sharp potholes can still damage wheels.

Nairobi traffic

Compact and easy to park, the GR Yaris is well suited to city streets. The automatic makes traffic far less tiring than the manual. The ride is firm over rough patches, though.

Highway cruising

Stable and quick, but road and engine noise are more noticeable than in a larger, more refined car. Long trips are entirely possible but more tiring than in a premium saloon.

Practicality and running costs in Kenya

Toyota is represented in Kenya by CFAO Mobility, and the brand's enormous local presence is a significant advantage. Many GR Yaris models in Kenya arrive as imports, so check with the franchise about warranty and parts for the specific car you are considering. Specialist components unique to the GR Yaris may need to be ordered.

  • Fuel: the GR Yaris requires premium petrol and is reasonably economical when driven gently, though enthusiastic driving increases consumption.
  • Tax: the 1.6-litre engine, at just over 1,500cc, falls into the 25% excise band for imported petrol cars.
  • Servicing: follow Toyota's severe-conditions schedule if you drive on gravel or dusty roads.
  • Tyres and brakes: performance tyres and brakes wear faster than those of an ordinary hatchback, but costs are far lower than for a supercar.
  • Value: strong demand and limited supply help support resale values.
Most performance cars avoid gravel. The GR Yaris goes looking for it.

Rivals

  • Volkswagen Golf R: more refined and practical, less engaging on loose surfaces.
  • Honda Civic Type R: brilliant front-wheel-drive hot hatch, but lacks all-wheel drive for gravel.
  • Toyota GR Corolla: shares the GR Yaris's drivetrain in a larger body, in selected markets.
  • BMW M3: far faster and more practical, at a much higher price.

Verdict

The GR Yaris is one of the most engaging cars on sale, and perhaps the one most perfectly suited to Kenya's mix of tarmac and murram. It is compact, rally-bred, mechanically robust and endlessly entertaining, with the backing of Toyota's local presence. Its firm ride, cramped rear and limited availability are minor complaints next to the joy it delivers. In the year Toyota's rally car conquered the Safari, its road-going cousin makes a compelling case of its own.
